newsitem.title: USA: Summit Technology fires founding chief executive.
newsitem.headline: Summit Technology fires founding chief executive.

text.p: Summit Technology Inc., a money-losing maker of laser systems to correct common vision disorders, said Friday that its board fired company founder David Muller as chairman and chief executive.

Dogged by a pair of government investigations, shareholder lawsuits and lingering scepticism over its vision correction technology, Summit said the board established a new executive committee chaired by President Verne Sharma, who will also serve as interim CEO.
The executive committee was formed to "identify and evaluate strategic options designed to achieve profitability," the company said in a statement.
Analysts applauded Muller's departure and Summit's stock, which traded as high as $38.75 in December, traded Friday afternoon up 25 cents at $6.06 on the Nasdaq market.
Muller founded Summit a decade ago after developing a laser that treats nearsightedness by slicing off a thin layer of the eye's cornea, which can eliminate the need for eyeglasses.
However, the surgical procedure, which costs about $1,700 to $2,000 per eye, has not been well received by potential patients and the company sold few of the machines to doctors.
"I think that David Muller gave a bad image to the company," said Anne Anderson, an analyst with Atlantis Investment. "I think investors are relieved he is leaving."
Muller could not be reached for comment.
Richard Miller, a board member speaking on behalf of the directors, said in a statement, "It is now time for the company to focus on the bottom line."

In April, Summit said Muller received in late 1995 a package of what appeared to be internal Food and Drug Administration documents on a laser eye system under development by arch-rival VISX Inc. Summit said the FDA was conducting an internal investigation of the security breach.
Several shareholders have since filed lawsuits, charging that Muller and other top officers at Summit, armed with the highly-confidential FDA material, sold millions of dollars in Summit stock.
Muller sold 107,000 shares in February and currenty holds about 1.3 million of the 31 million outstanding shares, Summit spokeswoman Paula Elliott said.
Last October Summit said the Federal Trade Commission had launched an investigation to determine whether it engaged in unfair competition against VISX.
"Possibly, the new management may be able to resolve or offload some of that (controversy) on David. It's not clear that the company may have been involved," Anderson said.
This year Summit opened 19 of its own vision correction centres across the country and installed another six of its eye lasers in teaching hospitals.

Elliott said most of the centres opened this summer and are not profitable. Summit, which also sells contact lens and related products through Lens Express Inc., has lost $15.5 million on revenues of $43.4 million during the first six months this year.
Analysts said Summit would likely reevaluate its expansion plans and may consider closing the vision correction centres.
"They're clearly losing money in the business," said Archie Smith of Piper Jaffrey. "Just cutting promotional activity ... can have a significant impact on their financials."
The centres have angered doctors who bought Summit's lasers, expecting to develop their own business and now find a competitor, and hurt new sales to doctors, Smith said.
Sharma joined Summit from U.S. Surgical Corp. earlier this year and analysts said they had little idea of how he would run Summit.
"He barely had time to get his feet wet. He's not someone the investment community has even met. This was David Muller's company," Anderson said.
